stem: Why are asymmetrical skin creases in the thigh or buttocks considered an unreliable 'hard sign' for DDH?

options.text: They only appear in children over $12$ months of age.
They are only visible in children with severe dislocations.
About $30\%$ of perfectly normal children have them.
They disappear when the child is placed in a flexed position.

explanation: Because a large percentage of healthy infants exhibit these creases, they cannot be used as a definitive diagnostic marker on their own.
rationale: Consider the frequency with which this sign appears in the healthy population.

optionExplanations.A: Skin creases are examined in infancy, but their presence does not correlate perfectly with hip pathology.
optionExplanations.B: Creases can be seen in various degrees of dysplasia, but their diagnostic value is limited by their commonality in healthy infants.
optionExplanations.C: Because a large percentage of healthy infants exhibit these creases, they cannot be used as a definitive diagnostic marker on their own.
optionExplanations.D: The source material focuses on the high prevalence of this sign in the normal population rather than its physical disappearance during movement.
